title: The Keepers' Rule
author: the Keepers of the Unsung Vault, each in turn
body:
# The Rule

*Knotted on a cord, and written out beside it on the wall in charcoal by somebody who could write.*

---

The Keeper sings the first voice.

The unsung cannot sing the second; that is why they are here. The Keeper sings it for them, after the first, and the third after that, and so the round goes round with one voice in it, which is not a round. It is the best that can be done.

A lantern that goes out is lit again from the Keeper's own, never from another. A lantern lit from another's is a borrowed name.

The Keeper does not listen to the floor.

*Under it, in a newer hand, much smaller:* It has started singing the second voice. It is very nearly right.

title: A Page on the Vault Steps
author: Aue Sa, the Keeper's apprentice
body:
# Tied to the first pole

*A page of birch-bark, weighted with a stone on the top step.*

---

If you are going down, do not sing. She will hear a round and think it is the one under the floor, and she will turn round to answer it.

If you are going down to put her to rest, I am sorry. I should have been the one. I was singing the second voice and I stopped when she stopped and I ran, and a Keeper's apprentice who stops singing is not anything any more.

Her lantern is the one on the long pole. All the others were lit from it. Bring it up to the light.

*A. S., who sleeps in the crannog, if anybody wants to shout at her.*

title: The Goose-Count
author: Eune Mor, goose-herd
body:
# Geese at the fold

*Knotted on a withy cord, one knot a goose, a red rush for a gander; read out loud by her grandson and written down by a passing clerk for a copper.*

---

First frost: forty-one down from the clans' country. Three ganders.

New moon: forty-one. They will not settle. They stand in the fold with their necks out like a row of oars, all of them facing west, and call, all night.

West is the carr. There is nothing in the carr but the Vault and the old crannog.

*The next knot is tied loose, which is how Eune marks a night she did not sleep:* Thirty-eight. The leech-hounds had three through the withies while I was on the deck singing. I will not stop singing. Somebody has to, and the geese can hear that it is not the right voice, and they come in anyway.

title: The Tide Turned Round
author: the Flood-Callers of Oulnauve
body:
# The Tide Turned Round

*Printed nowhere; painted in indigo on a strip of burial paper and nailed up in the stakes' yard.*

---

The world is a shore. The tide went out. Our grandmothers built stilts and waited and said: it will come back, and the drowned will walk.

They said it and they did nothing. They sent the dead out with lanterns *so that they would go out further*. Every lantern is a stone on the dead to keep them down. Every round sung at a jetty is a door shut.

We cut the lanterns. We do not sing. And the drowned come up, and every one that comes up is a wave, and when there are enough waves it is the flood.

We are not killing anybody. We are bringing them home.

*Scratched at the foot, in a different hand:* Aunsa says the bell next. All of them at once.

title: A Flood-Caller's Sounding
author: a Flood-Caller who dived for the Drowned Bell
body:
# Under the bell

*Written in a shaking hand on the back of a bundle-tag, wrapped in oilskin and pushed into the shrine's stones.*

---

Six fathoms by the knotted line. Black water, and then not black, because there is light down there, a little, the colour of a lantern at the very end of its oil.

The bell stands upright on the bottom. It is taller than a house and not ours. Nobody hung it; it stands.

They are round it. All of them. Three hundred years of the Delta's dead, standing on the bottom in rings round the bell, with their faces turned to it, and not one of them turned to look at me.

They are not waiting for a flood. They are waiting for the bell to say something.

I am not going to tell Aunsa this. I am going to leave it here and go home and sing.

title: A Page from the Tally Book
author: the clerks of the Eel Tally
body:
# The Guild's Tally, Delta Station

*A leaf torn from the back of the book, in two inks.*

---

| Landing | Barrels up | Tithe (one in ten) |
|---|---|---|
| Nauve's Landing | 610 | 61 |
| Moreva | 380 | 38 |
| Oulea (the Hurdles) | 400 | 40 |

*The same rows again underneath in brown ink, with the Oulea figure written as 440, and the tithe as 55, and a small tidy sum in the margin that goes nowhere in the book.*

*In the new clerk's hand across the bottom:* The trappers must keep their own count. Reedfolk always do. Find it before the next boat goes up. W. C.

title: Hester's List
author: Hester Wrenn, of Gosford and the Delta
body:
# The names

*A Vale almanac with the pages cut out and the covers kept, and a list written inside them in pencil gone over in ink.*

---

Jonah Coe, carter, Gosford. The Greyreed in flood, the year the ford went.

Annet Stall, drover's girl. Came down after her father. Found at the Reed Bridge.

A man with a Warden's buckle and no name. I called him Tom, because somebody should.

Piers Hollin. Ran from the barrow country. I knew his mother.

Will Wrenn, my brother. No. He is not in the water. He is in the Vale, and he does not write, and that is different.

*Last, in fresh ink, and then crossed through so hard the pen went through the page:* Hester Wrenn.

title: The Chair's Naming-Cord
author: the tenders of Isse's Chair
body:
# Named at the Chair

*A long cord of indigo rush, knotted, coiled on the seat; read out by the tender for anyone who asks.*

---

Every name said at the Chair is tied here: the married, two knots twisted together; the dead, one knot and a loop; the born, a knot and nothing after it, because nothing has happened to them yet.

The cord goes back to a knot nobody can read, tied in a rush that does not grow in the Delta, pale green, as if it had been cut out of the stone of the seat.

*The tender says:* That one is Isse. She tied it herself, before she sat down to teach them. It is a born knot. Nothing has happened to her yet.

title: The Leech-Wife's Ledger
author: Illa Nauve
body:
# Leeches and hounds

*Chalked on the inside of a kennel door and copied onto a board for anyone who buys.*

---

Tub one, the black-backs, for the bleeders at Isseva. Tub two, the striped, for bruising. Tub three, the old ones, for the Council, who pay.

Hounds: Mother (the old bitch). Reed, Rope, Sallow, Lantern, Bittern, and the three pups not named.

A hound that has been bitten by a leech learns to bite like one. I bred them to it; it keeps the herons off the tubs.

*Scratched after, with something sharper than chalk:* Mother slipped her collar at the thaw and went into the reeds. They all went after her. They come back every night now, and they do not come to the door.

title: The Pumping-Book
author: Gerent Voss, engineer to the Tallymen
body:
# West Delta Drainage, Station One

*An engineer's book in a brass-cornered case, swollen with damp, open at its last written page.*

---

Day 90. Wind WSW, steady. Lift: eleven hundred buckets. Level in the sump down four inches. The reedfolk still come and stand at the edge of the cut and sing. The Council was paid. I do not know what else they want.

Day 96. Lift: twelve hundred. The water is coming up clear now, and cold, and it tastes of iron and something like a struck bell. It is not the marsh's water. The marsh is brown.

Day 97. Lift: nine hundred. Level in the sump *up* two inches, against the wind, against the pump.

Day 98. Something is standing in the sump. I am going down.

*Nothing after that. The column of figures for Day 98 has been written in and then written over, again and again, until it is a black square.*

title: Rubbings from the Drylanders' Hummock
author: taken from the grave-boards west of Isseva
body:
# The boards

*Charcoal rubbings on reed paper, one board to a sheet.*

---

ODO FENWICK, CLERK TO THE GUILD. HE ASKED FOR THE EARTH AND GOT IT.

A WARDEN. HIS NAME WAS ON A ROLL THAT WENT TO THE WATER BEFORE HIM.

MARRA OF THE SALT ISLES, WHO SAID THE SEA HAD HAD ENOUGH OF HER FAMILY.

JONAH COE OF GOSFORD, CARTER. *(The lantern beside this one is Hester's weave, not a reedfolk one.)*

*The newest board, the letters careful, the cuts still pale:*

HESTER WRENN OF GOSFORD. SHE KNEW ALL THEIR NAMES.

*In front of it the earth has been dug and turned and left open, and there is nobody in it.*

title: The Bloomer's Cord
author: Kesse Lissa, bloomer
body:
# Blooms this spring

*A cord of rush knotted on the furnace's wicker door; a knot for each bloom of iron, a bead of slag threaded for each one that failed.*

---

Knot, knot, knot, bead, knot. The ore from the east pits is best this year, red as a heron's eye.

Knot, knot. Two eel-spears' worth for Oulea and the nails for Ollo's new hull.

The old pits have filled. Grandmother's pits, where the ore was cut out before I was born; they fill and the ore grows back in the water a hand's depth a lifetime, and something warm has found them now, from the furnace.

*The cord stops there. Tied round the last knot, a sallowjaw's tooth, and a knot that is not a bloom: the one for a person gone into the water.*

title: The Row-Knots of the Grey Line
author: the stake-drivers of Nauvissa
body:
# Sixty rows

*The knots of every row, read off by walking the line from the grey back to the village, as the stake-drivers do each midsummer.*

---

The first row: white rush, gone to nothing. The year of the Ash Winter. The grey came up the Greyreed as far as a boat goes in a morning.

The twentieth row: the year the South Stilts were raised. A reed-bed a year, every year, as the Council said.

The fortieth row: a reed-bed a year.

The sixtieth row, this midsummer's, a reed-bed from Nauvissa's back jetty: the knots were tied in green rush on the day.

*They have been tied again. The same knots, the same weave, in grey rush that crumbles when it is touched, and warm, the drivers say, as a hand.*

title: The Watchman's Log
author: the watchman of the South Stilts
body:
# Paid in eels

*Notches on the watch-house's door-post, and a note on birch-bark for the Council, which never came to read it.*

---

Twenty years on these stilts, and a notch for every day the grey did not move. The post is full; I started on the ladder.

The last ten notches are different. I have cut them twice: once at dusk, where the grey is when I climb up, and once at dawn, where it is when I climb down. They are not the same place.

It comes in at night. It goes back by day. I have told the Council. The Council has told me I am paid in eels.

I am going to drive a stake where it comes to tonight and see if the stake is grey in the morning.

title: A Rubbing from Isse's Stair
author: taken from the ninth step of the colonnade
body:
# Two hands on one step

*A charcoal rubbing, the paper gone soft with the wet.*

---

Across the riser of the ninth step, in the Builders' square marks that nobody reads: a line, and under it a longer line.

Under those, cut later and shallower, in the reedfolk's knot-letters, which were made to be tied and not cut and look wrong in stone:

ISSE CAME DOWN HERE INTO THE WATER AND WALKED ON THE BOTTOM TO THE LEANING HOUSE AND CAME BACK UP WITH THE STILTS.

*And beside it, smaller:* The Builders' line says the same. Isse. It is our word for water. It was theirs first.

title: The Feeders' Tally
author: the reedfolk who feed the Sallow King's sallowjaws
body:
# What the King's jaws were given

*Knotted on a cord hung from the lowest branch of the ring, well above where a sallowjaw can reach.*

---

The first of the thaw: three baskets of eel-heads, from Oulea.

Midsummer: a sheep, from a Vale drover who would not take it any further.

The new moon: nothing, because nobody came. They came up to the edge of the ring and looked out, and went back.

*The latest knot:* We are asked by the Council to remind anybody reading this cord that there is only one place in the marsh where the jaws are fed so that they will stay, and that you are standing in it, and that they are hungry.

title: A Stews-Keeper's Note to the Tally
author: the keeper of the Eel Stews
body:
# To the clerk at the Tally

*Folded small and wedged in the high pond's sluice-gate.*

---

Sir,

The high pond is empty again. The sluice was shut, I shut it myself, and the wall is wet on the outside and dry on the in. I do not know how you tally eels that have left, but I expect the Guild will tell me it is a deduction.

The Landing says a live eel is a reedfolk price and a dead one is yours. These were neither. They went out over the wall in the night and down the channel to the sea, the wrong way, all of them, and if you want them counted you may go and count them.

The keeper.

title: A Letter in the Chimney-Box
author: a mother of the drowned house
body:
# For whoever lights us

*In the strongbox wedged in the chimney, wrapped round a string of eel-bone beads.*

---

The ground went down under the house in the night and the water came up through the floor, and we stood on the table and then on the shelf and then there was no more house to stand on.

The chimney is stone. I am putting this in it.

We have no family in Isseva now. Nobody will measure the oil for us, or sing us out. If you find this, and you have a lantern, light it here, and sing any voice of the round you know, even badly. We will not mind which.

If you have no lantern, the lights over the water are not us. Do not follow them.

title: The Cutters' Finds-Book
author: Deo Oul and Lia Oul, peat-cutters
body:
# Found in the peat, and paid for

*A tally-board by the drying-stacks, with prices the finders are owed chalked beside each find.*

---

A bronze pin, the Builders' make. The Sayers pay for these by the ounce.

A wooden bowl with porridge still in it. Nobody will pay for this. Lia would not let me throw it away.

A dog, perfectly kept, with its collar on. Buried again, where it was.

A Warden in his coat, perfectly kept, with a roll of names in his hand. The Wardens want him and the Order wants him, and nobody wants to pay for him, and he is under a tarpaulin by the fire, and Lia talks to him in the evenings.

*In Lia's hand:* He listens.

title: The Shrine's Keeping
author: the families who keep the Drowned Bell Shrine
body:
# Midnight

*Cut into a board under the Hearthstone's lip, where the spray does not reach.*

---

At midnight the bell under the water tolls once. It has done it every night since before anybody's grandmother, and nobody hung it.

When it tolls, those who are keeping the shrine say one name of someone who went out from here, and do not say what they wish.

What they wish is that one night it will toll twice.
